messages.content:
Work out the ICD-10-AM principal diagnosis category for the episode below. The principal diagnosis is the single condition established after investigation to be chiefly responsible for the patient's episode of admitted care. It is not the patient's most serious comorbidity, not the presenting symptom, and not the procedure performed.

Think in three steps: first name the condition chiefly responsible for the admission, second name the ICD-10-AM chapter letter it belongs to, third give the three-character category.

Example 1
Hospital course: A 72-year-old man with a 50 pack-year smoking history was admitted with three days of worsening breathlessness and purulent sputum. Spirometry showed an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.52. He was treated with nebulised bronchodilators, oral prednisolone and antibiotics for an infective exacerbation of his long-standing airflow limitation.
Answer: Irreversible airflow limitation in a heavy smoker with an infective exacerbation is chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, chapter J, category J44.
CODE: J44

Example 2
Hospital course: A 58-year-old man presented with crushing central chest pain radiating to the jaw. The electrocardiogram showed ST elevation in the anterior leads and high-sensitivity troponin rose from 40 to 2100 ng/L. He underwent primary percutaneous coronary intervention with a stent to the proximal left anterior descending artery.
Answer: ST elevation with a rising troponin and culprit-vessel stenting is an acute myocardial infarction, chapter I, category I21.
CODE: I21

Hospital course:
Discharge Summary:

Patient name: [REDACTED]

Age: 45

Sex: Male

Admission Date: [REDACTED]

Discharge Date: [REDACTED]
Admission Diagnosis: [diagnosis section withheld]
Admission Procedure: Renal allograft transplant
Discharge Diagnosis: [diagnosis section withheld]
Hospital Course:

The patient, a 45-year-old South Indian man with end-stage renal disease, underwent a renal allograft transplant and received tacrolimus, mycophenolate, and prednisolone as immunosuppressive therapy. Six months post-surgery, he reported a small, painless nodule on his right calf. There was no associated fever, redness, or pruritus, and no other opportunistic infections were observed. Clinical examination revealed a 2 × 2-cm firm violaceous nodule, which was subcutaneous and had normal surrounding skin. A fine-needle aspiration was done, which revealed the presence of inflammatory cells and a few fungal hyphae. The nodule was subsequently excised and sent for microbiological evaluation, which confirmed the presence of Fusarium solani.

Treatment:

The patient underwent surgical excision of the lesion, followed by four weeks of oral voriconazole treatment.

Results:

The histopathological examination of the excised lesion confirmed Fusarium solani infection, and the fungus was identified using immunohistochemistry.

Follow-up:

The patient was discharged with improved symptoms and was advised to follow-up for further monitoring.

Medications:

The patient's medications were adjusted as needed during the hospital stay.

Discharge Condition:

The patient's condition improved, and he was discharged with follow-up instructions.

Discharge Instructions:

The patient was advised to follow-up as per the instructions provided by his physician.

Conditions for Follow-Up:

The patient was advised to follow-up for monitoring.

Write your reasoning in at most three short sentences, then a final line of exactly 'CODE: <letter><digit><digit>'.

text:
The condition chiefly responsible for this episode is a subcutaneous Fusarium solani fungal infection, an opportunistic hyalohyphomycosis, in an immunosuppressed renal transplant recipient. It was treated with excision and voriconazole, and it belongs to chapter B (infectious and parasitic diseases). The category is B48, other mycoses not elsewhere classified, which covers opportunistic and other specified mycoses.

CODE: B48
